records.title: Basic Calculator
records.vocabulary: Basic Calculator Scientific Calculator Core Workspaces Evaluates bracketed arithmetic expressions step by step.
records.definition: The Basic Calculator evaluates a typed arithmetic expression by following BODMAS, not left-to-right guessing. For (12 + 8) / 4 the brackets make 20 first, then division gives 5. Shop totals, recipe scaling, and shared fares all use the same ordered trace. A common error is reading 12 + 8 / 4 as 5; the live strip shows why brackets change the value.
records.formula:
Order of operations: brackets first, then division, then addition/subtraction. operation: the calculation step being applied
Order of operations: a+b\times c=a+(b\times c). Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the grouping.
records.example: Evaluate (18 − 6) × 2 + 4.: Brackets: 18 − 6 = 12. Multiply: 12 × 2 = 24. Add: 24 + 4 = 28. Use Order of operations: brackets first, then division, then addition/subtraction. Answer: 28

records.title: Fraction Calculator
records.vocabulary: Fraction Calculator Scientific Calculator Core Workspaces Simplifies fractions and performs fraction arithmetic with exact and decimal outputs.
records.definition: The Fraction Calculator adds 1/2 and 3/4 as exact parts. It rewrites 1/2 as 2/4, then adds only numerators to get 5/4, which is 1 1/4 or 1.25. Pizza slices, measuring cups, and shared prices use the same LCD bars. Adding denominators to make 4/6 is the error the labelled bars are built to stop.
records.formula:
Fraction value: a/b = a divided by b. a: numerator; b: non-zero denominator; b != 0
Order of operations: a+b\times c=a+(b\times c). Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the grouping.
records.example: Add 1/2 + 3/4.: LCD of 2 and 4 is 4. 1/2 = 2/4. 2/4 + 3/4 = 5/4. Use Fraction value: a/b = a divided by b. Answer: 5/4

records.title: Mixed Numbers
records.vocabulary: Mixed Numbers Scientific Calculator Core Workspaces Converts, compares and calculates with mixed numbers.
records.definition: Mixed Numbers writes a whole amount and a leftover part together, such as 2 1/3. That mark means 2 + 1/3, which is 7/3, not 2 × 1/3. Baking 2 1/2 cakes, cutting 3 1/4 metres of wood, and timing 1 1/2 hours all use this split. The blocks and strips show the whole rectangles and the leftover third side by side.
records.formula:
Mixed number value: a b/c = a + b/c. a: whole number; b: fraction numerator; c: non-zero denominator; c != 0
Order of operations: a+b\times c=a+(b\times c). Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the grouping.
records.example: Write 2 1/3 as an improper fraction.: 2 = 6/3. 6/3 + 1/3 = 7/3. The leftover third stays in the numerator. Use Mixed number value: a b/c = a + b/c. Answer: 7/3

records.title: Percentage Calculator
records.vocabulary: Percentage Calculator Scientific Calculator Core Workspaces Calculates percentage, percentage change, discounts, tax and reverse percentages.
records.definition: The Percentage Calculator reads p% as p hundredths of a base. 15% of 240 is (15/100)×240 = 36, shown on a hundred grid, a percent scale, and part/whole bars. Discounts, marks, and battery charge use the same three numbers: percent, base, and part. Using 15 instead of 0.15 is the error the grid is labelled to catch.
records.formula:
Percent of a number: p% of x = (p/100)x. p: percent value; x: base amount
Order of operations: a+b\times c=a+(b\times c). Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the grouping.
records.example: Find 15% of 240.: 15% = 15/100 = 0.15. 0.15 × 240 = 36. The part is 36. Use Percent of a number: p% of x = (p/100)x. Answer: 36

records.title: Ratio Calculator
records.vocabulary: Ratio Calculator Scientific Calculator Core Workspaces Simplifies ratios and divides quantities in a stated ratio.
records.definition: The Ratio Calculator compares two counts in the form a : b and then simplifies by their GCF. 8 : 12 becomes 2 : 3 because both parts divide by 4. The lab shows GCF groups, tape bars, a tile array, and a double number line. Recipe mixes, map keys, and class votes use the same simplified pair. Adding 8 + 12 and calling 20 the ratio is the labelled mistake.
records.formula:
Equivalent ratio: a:b = ka:kb. a: first part; b: second part; k: non-zero scale factor; k != 0
Order of operations: a+b\times c=a+(b\times c). Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the grouping.
records.example: Simplify 8 : 12.: gcd(8, 12) = 4. 8 ÷ 4 = 2 and 12 ÷ 4 = 3. The simplest ratio is 2 : 3. Answer: 2 : 3

records.title: Powers and Roots
records.vocabulary: Powers and Roots Scientific Calculator Core Workspaces Evaluates powers, square roots, cube roots and nth roots.
records.definition: Powers and Roots links a base-and-exponent product with the inverse root. 2^5 is five factors of 2, which is 32; the fifth root of 32 returns 2. Area grids show squares, a cube model shows 2^3 = 8, and the repeated-factor chain lists 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2. Growth of bacteria, pixel resolution, and side-from-area problems use the same pair of operations.
records.formula:
Square root: sqrt(a)=b means b^2=a. a: number under the root; b: principal square root; a >= 0 for real square roots
Order of operations: a+b\times c=a+(b\times c). Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the grouping.
records.example: Evaluate 2^5.: 2^5 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2. The product is 32. Five factors of 2 make 32. Use Square root: sqrt(a)=b means b^2=a. Answer: 32

records.title: Scientific Notation
records.vocabulary: Scientific Notation Scientific Calculator Core Workspaces Converts between ordinary and scientific notation and performs calculations.
records.definition: Scientific Notation writes a number as a coefficient times a power of ten, such as 4.5 × 10^{-4} for 0.00045. The coefficient stays at least 1 and less than 10 while the exponent counts the decimal-point shifts. Star distances, cell sizes, and calculator overflow all use this compact form. The number-line marker and shift arrows show each move of the point.
records.formula:
Scientific notation: N = a x 10^n. N: number; a: coefficient with 1 <= |a| < 10; n: integer exponent
Order of operations: a+b\times c=a+(b\times c). Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the grouping.
records.example: Write 0.00045 in scientific notation.: 0.00045 = 4.5 × 0.0001. 0.0001 = 10^{-4}. 0.00045 = 4.5 × 10^{-4}. Use Scientific notation: N = a x 10^n. Answer: 4.5 × 10^{-4}

records.title: Logarithms
records.vocabulary: Logarithms Scientific Calculator Core Workspaces Evaluates common, natural and custom-base logarithms.
records.definition: Logarithms undo exponentiation: log_b(a) is the exponent that raises b to a. So log_2(8) = 3 because 2^3 = 8. The power ladder, inverse-operation proof, and drag ranges keep base, exponent, and power in one picture. Earthquake scales, pH, and compound-growth inversion use the same undo step. A frequent slip is treating log as division by the base.
records.formula:
Log definition: log_b(x)=y means b^y=x. b: positive base not equal to 1; x: positive input; y: exponent; b > 0; b != 1; x > 0
Order of operations: a+b\times c=a+(b\times c). Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the grouping.
records.example: Evaluate log_2(8).: 2^3 = 8. The missing exponent is 3. log_2(8) = 3. Use Log definition: log_b(x)=y means b^y=x. Answer: 3

records.title: Exponential Calculations
records.vocabulary: Exponential Calculations Scientific Calculator Core Workspaces Calculates exponential expressions using adjustable base and exponent.
records.definition: Exponential Calculations follow a repeated-factor chain a^n and a growth chart. 2^6 is six doublings from 1, which is 64. The staircase animation, live factor list, and graded practice use the same base and exponent. Populations, compound interest, and pixel counts grow this way. Adding the exponent to the base, as in 2 + 6 = 8, is the labelled error.
records.formula:
Power: a^n = a x a x ... x a. a: base; n: number of factors
Order of operations: a+b\times c=a+(b\times c). Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the grouping.
records.example: Evaluate 2^6.: Start at 1. Double six times: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. 2^6 = 64. Use Power: a^n = a x a x ... x a. Answer: 64

records.title: Trigonometric Calculator
records.vocabulary: Trigonometric Calculator Scientific Calculator Core Workspaces Calculates sine, cosine, tangent and reciprocal ratios in degree or radian mode.
records.definition: The Trigonometric Calculator reads an angle on the unit circle and reports sine, cosine, and tangent. At 30° the point is (√3/2, 1/2), so sin 30° = 1/2. The dual-angle model, exact-value triangles, and DEG/RAD switch keep the same point. Ramps, circular motion, and bearings use these ratios. Mixing degrees with a radian formula is the labelled trap.
records.formula:
Right-triangle ratios: sin(theta)=opposite/hypotenuse, cos(theta)=adjacent/hypotenuse. theta: angle; opposite: side across from theta; hypotenuse: longest side
Order of operations: a+b\times c=a+(b\times c). Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the grouping.
records.example: Find sin 30°.: 30° is a special angle. The opposite side of the 30-60-90 triangle is half the hypotenuse. sin 30° = 1/2. Use Right-triangle ratios: sin(theta)=opposite/hypotenuse, cos(theta)=adjacent/hypotenuse. Answer: 1/2

records.title: Inverse Trigonometry
records.vocabulary: Inverse Trigonometry Scientific Calculator Core Workspaces Evaluates inverse sine, cosine and tangent with domain guidance.
records.definition: Inverse Trigonometry recovers an angle from a ratio. If sin θ = 1/2 and θ is the principal value, then θ = 30° or π/6. The sine-ratio slider, unit-circle ray, and principal-range band show why other angles such as 150° are not the calculator’s first answer. Survey heights and ramp design use this reverse look-up.
records.formula:
Inverse sine: sin^-1(r)=theta means sin(theta)=r. r: ratio between -1 and 1; theta: principal angle; -1 <= r <= 1
Order of operations: a+b\times c=a+(b\times c). Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the grouping.
records.example: Find the principal value of sin^{-1}(1/2).: sin 30° = 1/2. 30° lies in [−90°, 90°]. sin^{-1}(1/2) = 30°. Use Inverse sine: sin^-1(r)=theta means sin(theta)=r. Answer: 30°

records.title: Hyperbolic Functions
records.vocabulary: Hyperbolic Functions Scientific Calculator Core Workspaces Evaluates hyperbolic functions and their inverses.
records.definition: Hyperbolic Functions use exponentials: sinh x = (e^x − e^{−x})/2 and cosh x = (e^x + e^{−x})/2. At x = 0, sinh 0 = 0 and cosh 0 = 1. The dual-exponential curves, difference construction, and hyperbola context keep the identities visible. Catenary cables and some special-relativity maps use these functions. Treating sinh like ordinary sine of a circle angle is the named slip.
records.formula:
Hyperbolic sine: sinh(x)=(e^x-e^-x)/2. x: input value; e: Euler's constant
Order of operations: a+b\times c=a+(b\times c). Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the grouping.
records.example: Evaluate sinh 0.: e^0 = 1 and e^{−0} = 1. sinh 0 = (1 − 1)/2. sinh 0 = 0. Use Hyperbolic sine: sinh(x)=(e^x-e^-x)/2. Answer: 0

records.title: Factorial, Permutation and Combination
records.vocabulary: Factorial, Permutation and Combination Scientific Calculator Core Workspaces Calculates factorials, permutations and combinations.
records.definition: Factorial, Permutation and Combination count arrangements. 5! = 120, 5P2 = 20 ordered pairs, and 5C2 = 10 unordered pairs. Draggable slots, n and r inputs, and comparison cards keep the three formulas apart. Seating, passwords, and team selection use them. Using n! for an unordered team is the error the cards are labelled to catch.
records.formula:
Combination: nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!). n: total objects; r: objects chosen; 0 <= r <= n
Order of operations: a+b\times c=a+(b\times c). Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the grouping.
records.example: Evaluate 5!.: 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1. The product is 120. 5! = 120. Use Combination: nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!). Answer: 120

records.title: Absolute Value
records.vocabulary: Absolute Value Scientific Calculator Core Workspaces Evaluates absolute values and displays them on a number line.
records.definition: Absolute Value is distance from zero. |−7| = 7 and |7| = 7, shown by a signed point, its mirror, and a number-line arc. Temperatures below zero, bank debits, and error sizes use this nonnegative distance. Dropping the bars and keeping the sign is the labelled mistake.
records.formula:
Absolute value: |x| = distance from 0. x: number
Order of operations: a+b\times c=a+(b\times c). Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the grouping.
records.example: Evaluate |−7|.: −7 is 7 units left of 0. Distance is 7. |−7| = 7. Use Absolute value: |x| = distance from 0. Answer: 7

records.title: Rounding and Precision
records.vocabulary: Rounding and Precision Scientific Calculator Core Workspaces Rounds to decimal places or significant figures and displays approximation error.
records.definition: Rounding and Precision cuts a number to an agreed place and names the leftover error. 22/7 rounded to 2 decimal places is 3.14 because the next digit is 2, which is less than 5. The number-line zoom, next-digit flag, and error bar show why 3.15 would be the wrong 2-place report. Money, measurements, and calculator displays all choose a precision.
records.formula:
Rounding error bound: error <= half of one unit in the last place. error: maximum rounding difference
Order of operations: a+b\times c=a+(b\times c). Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the grouping.
records.example: Round 22/7 to 2 decimal places.: 22/7 = 3.142857… The third decimal digit is 2, which is less than 5. 2-place rounding is 3.14. Answer: 3.14

records.title: Constants Library
records.vocabulary: Constants Library Scientific Calculator Core Workspaces Inserts pi, e, golden ratio and other constants into calculations.
records.definition: The Constants Library stores high-precision names such as π, e, and the golden ratio φ. With π ≈ 3.14159 a circle of radius 2 has circumference 4π ≈ 12.566. Dedicated circle, exponential, and pentagon models, plus a precision slider, show why early rounding of π to 22/7 is only an approximation. Science formulas should keep the named constant until the last step.
records.formula:
Circle circumference: C = 2 pi r. C: circumference; pi: circle constant; r: radius
Order of operations: a+b\times c=a+(b\times c). Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the grouping.
records.example: A circle has radius 2. Find the exact circumference.: C = 2πr. C = 2π(2) = 4π. Leave π unexpanded. Use Circle circumference: C = 2 pi r. Answer: 4π

records.title: Calculation History
records.vocabulary: Calculation History Scientific Calculator Core Workspaces Stores, edits, duplicates and reruns previous calculations.
records.definition: Calculation History keeps each evaluated line so a later step can reuse an earlier result. If line 1 is 12 + 8 = 20 and line 2 is 20 ÷ 4 = 5, recalling line 2 must return 5, not 20. Pin, copy, inspect, and dependency-chain checks stop a learner from grabbing the wrong row. Multi-step homework and lab logs need this provenance.
records.formula:
Visible history count: count = number of stored rows. count: visible saved calculations
Order of operations: a+b\times c=a+(b\times c). Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the grouping.
records.example: History has 12 + 8 = 20 then 20 ÷ 4 = 5. What does row 2 recall?: Row 1 result is 20. Row 2 evaluates 20 ÷ 4. Row 2 recalls 5. Use Visible history count: count = number of stored rows. Answer: 5

records.title: Exact and Decimal Modes
records.vocabulary: Exact and Decimal Modes Scientific Calculator Core Workspaces Switches between exact fractions, radicals, symbolic forms and decimal approximations.
records.definition: Exact and Decimal Modes keep a radical such as √2 exact until a chosen number of decimal places is requested. √2 stays √2 in exact mode and becomes 1.41 when 2 decimal places are asked. The unit-square diagonal, number-line marker, and expansion table show the leftover error. Mixing 1.41 back into an exact proof is the labelled mistake.
records.formula:
Exact versus decimal: sqrt(2) is exact; 1.414... is approximate. sqrt(2): exact irrational value
Order of operations: a+b\times c=a+(b\times c). Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the grouping.
records.example: Write √2 in exact mode.: The diagonal of a unit square is √2. Exact mode keeps the radical. The exact value is √2. Answer: √2

records.title: Algebra Workspace
records.vocabulary: Algebra Workspace Algebra and Dynamic Variables Core Workspaces Displays numbers, variables, expressions, equations, functions, points and dependent objects.
records.definition: Algebra Workspace stores named rules such as y = 2x + 3 and updates every dependent output when x moves. At x = 4, substitution gives y = 11. The dependency graph, live table, and parsed-rule checks keep the arrows honest. Price formulas and science relations are the same idea. Editing one node but not its dependents is the named error.
records.formula:
Equivalent expressions: A = B iff A-B = 0. A: first expression; B: second expression
Linear function: f(x)=mx+b. The slope m controls steepness and the intercept b shifts the graph vertically.
records.example: Expand 4(x + 3) in the workspace.: 4(x + 3) = 4·x + 4·3. 4·3 = 12. The expanded rule is 4x + 12. Use Equivalent expressions: A = B iff A-B = 0. Answer: 4x + 12

records.title: Variable Explorer
records.vocabulary: Variable Explorer Algebra and Dynamic Variables Core Workspaces Defines variables and updates all dependent objects instantly.
records.definition: Variable Explorer isolates one slider x and shows every linked stage: input, rule y = 2x + 3, substitution, and output. At x = −2 the chain is 2(−2) + 3 = −1. The dependency graph and value table update together. Ticket totals and recipe yields are the same one-source idea. Changing x in only one box is the labelled fault.
records.formula:
Substitution: f(c)=f(x) with x=c. x: variable; c: chosen value
Linear function: f(x)=mx+b. The slope m controls steepness and the intercept b shifts the graph vertically.
records.example: Evaluate 3x + 5 when x = −2.: x = −2. 3(−2) + 5 = −6 + 5. The value is −1. Use Substitution: f(c)=f(x) with x=c. Answer: −1

records.title: Numeric Sliders
records.vocabulary: Numeric Sliders Algebra and Dynamic Variables Core Workspaces Creates adjustable numeric parameters with min, max and step settings.
records.definition: Numeric Sliders let x move continuously inside a chosen range with a chosen step. With y = 2x + 3, moving x from 2 to 2.1 raises y from 7 to 7.2. The live substitution strip, pattern chips, and coordinate graph share one x. Volume knobs and sensor readouts behave the same way. Ignoring the step and typing 2.13 when step is 0.1 is the labelled error.
records.formula:
Slider output: y = ax + b. a: slider-controlled parameter; x: input; b: constant
Linear function: f(x)=mx+b. The slope m controls steepness and the intercept b shifts the graph vertically.
records.example: If y = 2x + 3 and x = 2, find y.: 2(2) + 3 = 7. The linked result is 7. y = 7. Use Slider output: y = ax + b. Answer: 7

records.title: Integer Sliders
records.vocabulary: Integer Sliders Algebra and Dynamic Variables Core Workspaces Restricts slider values to integers for sequences, polygons and counting.
records.definition: Integer Sliders snap x to whole numbers only. For y = 2x + 3 the staircase visits (0, 3), (1, 5), (2, 7), (3, 9). Previous/next buttons, tick clicks, and the iteration table refuse 2.5. Counting people, floors, and discrete time steps need this snap. Treating the graph as a solid line without the corners is the labelled mistake.
records.formula:
Integer step: next value = current value + k. k: integer step size
Linear function: f(x)=mx+b. The slope m controls steepness and the intercept b shifts the graph vertically.
records.example: For y = 2x + 3 and integer x = 3, find y.: 2(3) + 3 = 9. The selected lattice point is (3, 9). y = 9. Use Integer step: next value = current value + k. Answer: 9

records.title: Angle Sliders
records.vocabulary: Angle Sliders Algebra and Dynamic Variables Core Workspaces Adjusts angles in degrees or radians and drives rotations or trig models.
records.definition: Angle Sliders turn a handle around the unit circle and report degrees, radians, and sine. At 90° the ray is on the positive y-axis, the sine-wave probe is at 1, and the radian reading is π/2. Common-angle chips jump to 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°. Gears, clocks, and bearings share this control. Mixing a degree number into a radian sine formula is the labelled trap.
records.formula:
Full turn: 360 degrees = 2 pi radians. pi: circle constant
Linear function: f(x)=mx+b. The slope m controls steepness and the intercept b shifts the graph vertically.
records.example: Convert 90° to radians.: θ_rad = 90 × π/180. 90/180 = 1/2. The radian measure is π/2. Use Full turn: 360 degrees = 2 pi radians. Answer: π/2

records.title: Animation Controls
records.vocabulary: Animation Controls Algebra and Dynamic Variables Core Workspaces Animates sliders and objects with play, pause, speed and direction controls.
records.definition: Animation Controls play a parameter through frames. A run from 1 to 9 in steps of 2 shows the five frames 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. Play/pause, speed, loop, and timeline seeking keep the same affine samples on the graph. Motion paths and time-based labs need this clock. Counting the last frame twice when looping is the labelled error.
records.formula:
Animated linear model: y = ax + 1. a: the animated slope parameter; x: the chosen input; 1: the fixed y-intercept; This lesson animates 0 <= a <= 2.; At x = 2, the exact output is y(2) = 2a + 1.
Linear function: f(x)=mx+b. The slope m controls steepness and the intercept b shifts the graph vertically.
records.example: An animation runs from 1 to 9 in steps of 2. How many frames?: The values are 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. n = (9 − 1)/2 + 1 = 5. There are 5 frames. Use Animated linear model: y = ax + 1. Answer: 5

records.title: Dependent and Independent Objects
records.vocabulary: Dependent and Independent Objects Algebra and Dynamic Variables Core Workspaces Shows which objects are free, dependent or auxiliary.
records.definition: Dependent and Independent Objects mark parents that you drag and children that you cannot type. If A and B are free points, the midpoint M = ((x_A + x_B)/2, (y_A + y_B)/2) and the segment length update when either parent moves. From A = (0, 0) and B = (4, 2), M is (2, 1) and length is √20. Locked child fields show the dependency. Editing M directly would break the definition.
records.formula:
Dependency: y = f(x). x: independent value; y: dependent value
Linear function: f(x)=mx+b. The slope m controls steepness and the intercept b shifts the graph vertically.
records.example: A = (0, 0), B = (4, 2). Find the midpoint.: M_x = (0 + 4)/2 = 2. M_y = (0 + 2)/2 = 1. M = (2, 1). Use Dependency: y = f(x). Answer: (2, 1)

records.title: Conditional Visibility
records.vocabulary: Conditional Visibility Algebra and Dynamic Variables Core Workspaces Shows or hides objects based on Boolean conditions or learner actions.
records.definition: Conditional Visibility shows or hides an object from a Boolean test on x. If the rule is x > 2, the number line lights the open ray (2, ∞) and the object is visible only there. Two sliders, six operators, and a before/after proof keep the boundary honest. Dashboard alerts and geometry hide/show rules use the same test. Including the endpoint when the operator is > is the labelled error.
records.formula:
Condition: show object if x > c. x: current value; c: threshold
Linear function: f(x)=mx+b. The slope m controls steepness and the intercept b shifts the graph vertically.
records.example: For the rule x > 2, is the object visible at x = 2?: x = 2 does not satisfy x > 2. The endpoint is open. The object is hidden. Use Condition: show object if x > c. Answer: hidden

records.title: Dynamic Labels
records.vocabulary: Dynamic Labels Algebra and Dynamic Variables Core Workspaces Displays live names, coordinates, values, measurements and equations.
records.definition: Dynamic Labels print a live string from coordinates. A point at (3, 4) can show the template “P(x, y)” as P(3, 4) and the distance template as 5. Token chips, steppers, and projection toggles keep the printed text equal to the calculated values. Maps and construction captions use this. Leaving a stale “P(3, 4)” after the point moved to (6, 8) is the labelled fault.
records.formula:
Dynamic text: label = name + value. name: fixed text; value: linked changing value
Linear function: f(x)=mx+b. The slope m controls steepness and the intercept b shifts the graph vertically.
records.example: Point P = (3, 4). What does the template P(x, y) print?: x = 3 and y = 4. Replace the tokens. The label is P(3, 4). Use Dynamic text: label = name + value. Answer: P(3, 4)

records.title: Algebraic Input
records.vocabulary: Algebraic Input Algebra and Dynamic Variables Core Workspaces Creates functions, equations, coordinates, lists and commands from an input bar.
records.definition: Algebraic Input parses a typed function, samples it, and names key points. For f(x) = x^2 − 4 the graph crosses the x-axis at −2 and 2, the y-intercept is −4, and the vertex is (0, −4). Syntax checks, create/edit/clear, and the sampled plot refuse a broken string. Science formulas start the same way. Typing 2x = 4 when a function of x was asked is the labelled mix-up.
records.formula:
Expression input: expression = terms joined by operations. term: number, variable, or product
Linear function: f(x)=mx+b. The slope m controls steepness and the intercept b shifts the graph vertically.
records.example: For f(x) = x^2 − 4, find the roots.: x^2 − 4 = 0. (x − 2)(x + 2) = 0. x = 2 or x = −2. Use Expression input: expression = terms joined by operations. Answer: x = −2, 2

records.title: Object Redefinition
records.vocabulary: Object Redefinition Algebra and Dynamic Variables Core Workspaces Changes definitions while preserving valid dependencies.
records.definition: Object Redefinition keeps the same object name while swapping its rule. At x = 4, y_old = 2x + 1 = 9 and y_new = 3x − 2 = 10, so the identity “y” jumps by 1. Dual graphs, the dependency tree, and the redefine transaction show dependents updating. Construction software uses this when a circle’s radius definition changes. Making a second object instead of redefining the first is the labelled confusion.
records.formula:
New rule: old object -> new definition. old object: existing object; new definition: replacement rule
Linear function: f(x)=mx+b. The slope m controls steepness and the intercept b shifts the graph vertically.
records.example: At x = 4, redefine y from 2x + 1 to 3x − 2. Find both values.: y_old = 2(4) + 1 = 9. y_new = 3(4) − 2 = 10. Δy = 1. Use New rule: old object -> new definition. Answer: old y = 9; new y = 10

records.title: Equation Input
records.vocabulary: Equation Input Algebra and Dynamic Variables Core Workspaces Accepts explicit, implicit, parametric and polar equations.
records.definition: Equation Input parses two sides joined by “=”. For 2x + 3 = 11 the equal-operation steps subtract 3 then divide by 2 to get x = 4, and the balance weights plus the dual-graph intersection both show that solution. Implicit multiplication, examples, and a substitution checklist keep 2x written as 2 × x. Typing only 2x + 3 with no equals sign is the labelled error.
records.formula:
Linear equation: ax+b=c. a: non-zero coefficient; b: constant; c: right side; a != 0
Linear function: f(x)=mx+b. The slope m controls steepness and the intercept b shifts the graph vertically.
records.example: Solve 2x + 3 = 11.: Subtract 3: 2x = 8. Divide by 2: x = 4. Check: 2(4) + 3 = 11. Use Linear equation: ax+b=c. Answer: x = 4

records.title: Inequality Input
records.vocabulary: Inequality Input Algebra and Dynamic Variables Core Workspaces Plots and shades one-variable and two-variable inequalities.
records.definition: Inequality Input parses a typed comparison such as 2x + 3 > 11. Subtracting 3 and dividing by 2 yields the open ray x > 4. The number line keeps a hollow dot at 4 because equality is not allowed. Temperature alerts and spending limits use the same open cut. Typing 2x+3 without an operator is the labelled error.
records.formula:
Linear inequality: ax+b<c. a: non-zero coefficient; b: constant; c: comparison value; flip the sign only when multiplying or dividing by a negative
Linear function: f(x)=mx+b. The slope m controls steepness and the intercept b shifts the graph vertically.
records.example: Solve 2x+3>11.: Subtract 3: 2x>8. Divide by 2: x>4. Open ray from 4. Answer: x>4

records.title: Lists
records.vocabulary: Lists Algebra and Dynamic Variables Core Workspaces Creates, transforms, sorts and applies operations to lists.
records.definition: Lists stores an ordered row such as [3, 5, 7, 9] whose sum is 24 and whose mean is 6. Dragging, appending, sorting, and mapping all act on that same ordered object. Score sheets and data columns use lists. Treating the list as an unordered bag loses the index 2 value 5.
records.formula:
List length: length = number of entries. length: count of list items
Linear function: f(x)=mx+b. The slope m controls steepness and the intercept b shifts the graph vertically.

records.title: Matrices

records.title: Cartesian Graphing
records.vocabulary: Cartesian Graphing 2D Graphing Calculator Graphs and Functions Plots functions, equations, points and datasets on an x-y plane.
records.definition: Cartesian Graphing places a labelled point such as (3,2) on perpendicular axes. Tick labels, quadrant names, and the origin stay visible. Maps and scatter plots use this plane. Swapping 3 and 2 to plot (2,3) is the labelled axis-order error.
records.formula:
Point rule: (x,y). x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: Plot (3,2). How far right of the origin?: x=3. 3 units right. The x-shift is 3. Answer: 3

records.title: Function Plotter
records.vocabulary: Function Plotter 2D Graphing Calculator Graphs and Functions Plots and styles several functions simultaneously.
records.definition: Function Plotter samples y=x^2−4, crossing the x-axis at −2 and 2 and sitting at the vertex (0,−4). The window and sample count control the smoothness. Science graphs start here. Plotting x=y^2 as if it were a function of x is the labelled mix-up.
records.formula:
Function rule: y=f(x). x: input; y: output
Transformation: y=a f(x)+b. The multiplier a stretches or reflects the graph; b shifts it up or down.
records.example: Find roots of y=x^2-4.: x^2=4. x=±2. The roots are -2 and 2. Answer: x=±2

records.title: Equation Grapher
records.vocabulary: Equation Grapher 2D Graphing Calculator Graphs and Functions Plots equations including forms not solved for y.
records.definition: Equation Grapher draws y=2x+3 and y=11 so they meet at (4,11). That x=4 is the solution of 2x+3=11. Implicit curves use the same idea. Reading only the y-intercept 3 as the solution is the labelled error. Equation Grapher keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Line equation: y=mx+b. m: slope; b: y-intercept
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: Solve 2x+3=11 by intersection.: Set 2x+3=11. x=4. The meet is (4,11). Answer: (4,11)

records.title: Inequality Grapher
records.vocabulary: Inequality Grapher 2D Graphing Calculator Graphs and Functions Shades half-planes and solution regions for inequalities.
records.definition: Inequality Grapher shades y<2x+1 below a dashed line. The test point (0,0) is inside because 0<1. Feasible regions in linear programming use this shade. Including the dashed line in the solution is the labelled error. Inequality Grapher keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Half-plane test: test a point in y<mx+b. x: test x-coordinate; y: test y-coordinate
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: Is (0,0) in y<2x+1?: 0<1 is true. (0,0) is inside. The test point works. Answer: yes

records.title: Parametric Curves
records.vocabulary: Parametric Curves 2D Graphing Calculator Graphs and Functions Plots x(t), y(t) with adjustable parameter intervals.
records.definition: Parametric Curves traces x=cos t, y=sin t so t=0 is (1,0) and t=π/2 is (0,1). The speed is the derivative pair, not the drawn radius. Orbits and animations use a parameter. Treating t as a third plotted axis is the labelled mistake.
records.formula:
Parametric point: x=f(t), y=g(t). t: parameter; x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: At t=0 for (cos t, sin t), where is the point?: cos0=1, sin0=0. The point is (1,0). On the x-axis. Answer: (1,0)

records.title: Polar Graphs
records.vocabulary: Polar Graphs 2D Graphing Calculator Graphs and Functions Plots equations using polar coordinates.
records.definition: Polar Graphs draws r=2 cos θ, a circle of diameter 2. At θ=0, r=2; at θ=π/2, r=0. Radar and rose curves use (r,θ). Plotting r as a Cartesian y against θ as x without converting is the labelled error. Polar Graphs keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Polar point: (r,theta). r: distance from origin; theta: direction angle
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: For r=2cosθ, find r at θ=0.: 2cos0=2. The point is 2 on the x-axis. r=2. Answer: 2

records.title: Point Plotter
records.vocabulary: Point Plotter 2D Graphing Calculator Graphs and Functions Plots individual points and point lists.
records.definition: Point Plotter drops listed samples such as (1,2), (2,5), (4,8). Each point keeps its own label. Survey marks and click-to-place labs use this list. Connecting the points and calling the polyline y=f(x) without a rule is the labelled slip.
records.formula:
Point: P=(x,y). x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: A list has (1,2) then (2,5). What is the second point?: Index 2 is (2,5). x=2, y=5. The point is (2,5). Answer: (2,5)

records.title: Data Plotter
records.vocabulary: Data Plotter 2D Graphing Calculator Graphs and Functions Plots imported or manually entered paired data.
records.definition: Data Plotter charts the sample 2, 5, 5, 8. The mean and the repeated 5 are both 5, shown as bars and dots. Lab measurements use this view. Plotting the index as if it were the value 2,3,4,5 is the labelled error. Data Plotter keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Data point: (input, output). input: explanatory value; output: measured value
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: Find the mean of 2,5,5,8.: Sum=20. 20/4=5. The mean is 5. Answer: 5

records.title: Table of Values
records.vocabulary: Table of Values 2D Graphing Calculator Graphs and Functions Generates editable x-y tables connected to plotted functions.
records.definition: Table of Values fills y=2x+3 at x=0,1,2,3 to get 3,5,7,9. Each row is a substitution, not a guess from the graph. Programming traces use tables. Skipping x=2 and writing 8 is the labelled arithmetic slip. Table of Values keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Table value: y=f(x). x: input; y: output
Transformation: y=a f(x)+b. The multiplier a stretches or reflects the graph; b shifts it up or down.
records.example: For y=2x+3, find y at x=2.: 2(2)+3=7. The pair is (2,7). y=7. Answer: 7

records.title: Trace Mode
records.vocabulary: Trace Mode 2D Graphing Calculator Graphs and Functions Tracks moving points or graph positions and optionally leaves traces.
records.definition: Trace Mode slides a probe on y=2x+3 so x=2 shows y=7. The readout is the sample at that x, not a free guess. Oscilloscope-style labs use a trace. Reporting y=6 at x=2 is the labelled mismatch. Trace Mode keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Trace point: (x,f(x)). x: selected input; f(x): output on the graph
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: Trace y=2x+3 at x=2. What is y?: 2(2)+3=7. The probe reads 7. y=7. Answer: 7

records.title: Zoom and Pan
records.vocabulary: Zoom and Pan 2D Graphing Calculator Graphs and Functions Supports pinch, wheel, rectangle zoom and panning.
records.definition: Zoom and Pan widens a view from [−2,2] to [−8,8] so more of y=x^2 appears, but the vertex stays (0,0). Maps use the same windowing. Thinking zoom changes the formula to y=4x^2 is the labelled error. Zoom and Pan keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Window width: xMax-xMin. xMax: right edge; xMin: left edge
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: A window [-2,2] zooms to [-8,8]. What is the new width?: 8-(-8)=16. Old width was 4. Width×4. Answer: 16

records.title: Axis Controls
records.vocabulary: Axis Controls 2D Graphing Calculator Graphs and Functions Changes ranges, scale ratios, labels, ticks and axis visibility.
records.definition: Axis Controls changes the tick step from 1 to 2 to 5. On [0,10] a step of 2 prints six labels. Log axes change the spacing, not the data values. Reading a log tick 100 as 2 because it is the second mark is the labelled error.
records.formula:
Axis interval: max-min. max: largest shown value; min: smallest shown value
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: Tick step 2 on [0,10]. How many labels?: 0,2,4,6,8,10. Six labels. Count is 6. Answer: 6

records.title: Grid Controls
records.vocabulary: Grid Controls 2D Graphing Calculator Graphs and Functions Switches Cartesian, polar and isometric grids and snap settings.
records.definition: Grid Controls turns minor lines on at 0.5 when majors sit at 1. Counting cells still uses the axis scale, not the number of lines. Engineering paper uses this. Counting 20 minor lines and calling the width 20 is the labelled scale error.
records.formula:
Grid step: next line = current line + step. step: grid spacing
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: Major 1, minor 0.5 on [0,2]. How many minor lines inside?: At 0.5 and 1.5. Two interior minors. Not counting the majors. Answer: 2

records.title: Multiple Graphics Views
records.vocabulary: Multiple Graphics Views 2D Graphing Calculator Graphs and Functions Shows two coordinated graphics views with independent settings.
records.definition: Multiple Graphics Views shows y=x^2 in a tight window [−2,2] and a wide window [−8,8]. The vertex is (0,0) in both. Linked cameras in geometry use this. Editing a copy in B that does not move A is the labelled desync. Multiple Graphics Views keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Same object: view1(object)=view2(object). object: shared mathematical item
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: View A is [-2,2], view B is [-8,8]. Is the vertex of y=x^2 the same?: Both show (0,0). One object. Yes. Answer: yes

records.title: Special Points
records.vocabulary: Special Points 2D Graphing Calculator Graphs and Functions Calculates roots, extrema, intersections and selected discontinuities.
records.definition: Special Points marks the roots ±2 and the vertex (0,−4) of y=x^2−4. Each mark is calculated from the formula, not clicked by eye. Optimisation graphs use these marks. Calling (1,−3) a vertex is the labelled error. Special Points keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Root condition: f(x)=0. x: root input; f(x): output
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: List special points of y=x^2-4.: Roots ±2. Vertex (0,-4). Three special points. Answer: (-2,0),(2,0),(0,-4)

records.title: Graph Inspector
records.vocabulary: Graph Inspector 2D Graphing Calculator Graphs and Functions Displays coordinates, function values, slope, tangent and curvature information.
records.definition: Graph Inspector reads y=2x+3 at x=3 as y=9 with slope 2. The panel is a calculator, not a hover guess. CAD inspect tools work this way. Showing y=8 at x=3 is the labelled readout error. Graph Inspector keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Point readout: selected point = (x,y). x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: Inspect y=2x+3 at x=3.: y=9. Slope 2. Readout (3,9). Answer: 9

records.title: Dynamic Parameters
records.vocabulary: Dynamic Parameters 2D Graphing Calculator Graphs and Functions Connects graphs to sliders and updates them continuously.
records.definition: Dynamic Parameters slides a in y=ax+3. At x=2, a=1 gives 5 and a=2 gives 7. Every linked object that reads a updates. Family plots use this. Changing a in the formula text but not the slider is the labelled split-state error.
records.formula:
Linear parameter: y=ax+b. a: slope parameter; b: intercept parameter
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: For y=ax+3 at x=2, a=1, find y.: 1*2+3=5. y=5. The value is 5. Answer: 5

records.title: Export Graph
records.vocabulary: Export Graph 2D Graphing Calculator Graphs and Functions Exports images, SVG, PDF-ready graphics or shareable activities.
records.definition: Export Graph saves the current window as 800×600 pixels. The axis numbers stay the data window, not 800. Reports and slides use the file. Thinking the x-axis now runs to 800 is the labelled pixel-data mix-up. Export Graph keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Exported view: export = graph + axes + labels + scale. graph: visible plotted object; scale: axis units
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: An 800×600 export of window [-2,2]×[-2,2]: what is the x-max in data?: x-max is still 2. 800 is pixels. 2. Answer: 2

records.title: Algebra Tiles
records.vocabulary: Algebra Tiles Expressions and Manipulation Algebra Uses positive and negative tiles for constants and variable terms.
records.definition: Algebra Tiles builds 2x+3 as two x-strips and three units, then combines 3x and −x to 2x. Shopping boxes and seat rows use the same grouping. Joining an x-tile to a unit as if they match is the labelled unlike-tile error.
records.formula:
Combine like tiles: 2x + 3x = 5x. x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; Do not combine unlike tiles.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.
records.example: Tiles for 2x+3: how many unit tiles?: 3 unit tiles. And two x-tiles. 3. Answer: 3

records.title: Like Terms
records.vocabulary: Like Terms Expressions and Manipulation Algebra Groups matching tiles and simplifies expressions.
records.definition: Like Terms collects 3x+5x into 8x and 7y−2y+4 into 5y+4. Taxi per-km charges add this way. Adding 2x+2y to 4xy is the labelled mixed-letter error. Like Terms keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Like terms: ax + bx = (a + b)x. x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; Variables and powers must match exactly.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.
records.example: Simplify 3x+5x.: 8x. Add coefficients. 8x. Answer: 8x

records.title: Substitution
records.vocabulary: Substitution Expressions and Manipulation Algebra Updates expression values from sliders or entered substitutions.
records.definition: Substitution puts x=4 into 2x+1 to get 9 and a=2 into 3a−5 to get 1. Bills and science formulas use this. Writing −3² = −9 instead of (−3)² = 9 is the labelled bracket error. Substitution keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Substitution: f(a) means replace x by a. x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; Use the same given value every time that variable appears.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.
records.example: Evaluate 2x+1 at x=4.: 8+1=9. 9. 9. Answer: 9

records.title: Expanding Brackets
records.vocabulary: Expanding Brackets Expressions and Manipulation Algebra Uses area models and symbolic steps.
records.definition: Expanding Brackets multiplies 4 through x+3 to 4x+12 and −2 through x−5 to −2x+10. Area of a split rectangle uses this. Multiplying only the first inside term is the labelled half-distribute error. Expanding Brackets keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Distributive law: a(b + c) = ab + ac. x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; Use the same outside factor for all terms inside.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.

records.title: Double Brackets
records.vocabulary: Double Brackets Expressions and Manipulation Algebra Builds rectangles whose partitions match expanded terms.
records.definition: Double Brackets expands (x+2)(x+3) into x²+5x+6 and (x+4)(x−4) into x²−16. Garden sides x+2 and x+3 use the four-area picture. Multiplying only first and last terms is the labelled missing-middle error. Double Brackets keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Double distribution: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd. x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; Keep signs attached to terms.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.
records.example: Expand (x+2)(x+3).: x^2+5x+6. FOIL. x^2+5x+6. Answer: x^2+5x+6

records.title: Factorisation
records.vocabulary: Factorisation Expressions and Manipulation Algebra Groups terms and rebuilds products or algebra-tile rectangles.
records.definition: Factorisation splits x²+5x+6 into (x+2)(x+3) and x²−9 into a difference of squares. Graph roots use the factors. Stopping without expanding back to check is the labelled unchecked-factor error. Factorisation keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Factor check: expand(factors) = original expression. x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; Factor over the intended number set.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.

records.title: Algebraic Fractions
records.vocabulary: Algebraic Fractions Expressions and Manipulation Algebra Simplifies and performs operations with domain restrictions.
records.definition: Algebraic Fractions cancels (x²−1)/(x−1) to x+1 with x≠1, and bars x=2 in (x+1)/(x−2). Speed formulas use this. Cancelling the x in (x+2)/x is the labelled term-not-factor error. Algebraic Fractions keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Denominator restriction: denominator != 0. denominator: the original denominator expression
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.
records.example: What value is excluded from (x+1)/(x-2)?: x-2=0. x=2. 2. Answer: 2

records.title: Indices
records.vocabulary: Indices Expressions and Manipulation Algebra Animates repeated multiplication and exponent-rule transformations.
records.definition: Indices adds 3+4 for x³x⁴ = x⁷ and multiplies 2×3 for (x²)³ = x⁶. Squares, cubes, and growth use powers. Adding indices on x²y³ to get xy⁵ is the labelled different-base error. Indices keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Product of powers: x^a x^b = x^(a+b). x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; Use index laws only when their conditions match.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.
records.example: Simplify x^3×x^4.: x^7. Add exponents. x^7. Answer: x^7

records.title: Surds
records.vocabulary: Surds Expressions and Manipulation Algebra Simplifies radicals and compares exact and decimal forms.
records.definition: Surds pulls the square 9 out of √18 to leave 3√2, then adds √8+√2 as 3√2. Tile diagonals stay exact. Writing √(9+16)=3+4 is the labelled split-over-sum error. Surds keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Product rule for roots: sqrt(ab) = sqrt(a)sqrt(b). x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; Keep radicands non-negative in this school setting.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.

records.title: Rationalisation
records.vocabulary: Rationalisation Expressions and Manipulation Algebra Shows conjugate multiplication step by step.
records.definition: Rationalisation multiplies 1/√2 by √2/√2 to get √2/2, and uses the conjugate on 1/(√3−1). Exact slopes use this. Multiplying only the denominator is the labelled unbalanced-1 error. Rationalisation keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Rationalising step: 1/sqrt(a) = sqrt(a)/a. x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; The multiplier must be non-zero.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.
records.example: Rationalise 1/√2.: √2/2. Multiply by √2/√2. √2/2. Answer: √2/2

records.title: Polynomial Operations
records.vocabulary: Polynomial Operations Expressions and Manipulation Algebra Adds, subtracts, multiplies and divides polynomial expressions.
records.definition: Polynomial Operations lines up like powers so x²+3x plus 2x²−x is 3x²+2x, and (x+1)(x+2) is x²+3x+2. Motion formulas use this. Adding x²+x as 2x² is the labelled unlike-power error. Polynomial Operations keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Polynomial addition: ax^n + bx^n = (a+b)x^n. x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; Powers in polynomials are non-negative whole numbers.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.
records.example: Add (x^2+3x)+(2x^2-x).: 3x^2+2x. Like terms. 3x^2+2x. Answer: 3x^2+2x

records.title: Synthetic Division
records.vocabulary: Synthetic Division Expressions and Manipulation Algebra Displays synthetic-division rows and resulting quotient.
records.definition: Synthetic Division uses a=−2 on 1,5,6 to get remainder 0 and quotient x+3. Root checks use this shortcut. Using +2 for divisor x+2 is the labelled sign error. Synthetic Division keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Remainder link: f(a) = remainder when dividing by x - a. x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; Use only for a linear divisor x - a in this lesson.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.
records.example: Divide x^2+5x+6 by x+2 using synthetic  -2.: Coefficients 1,5,6. Bring 1, 1×-2=-2, 3, 3×-2=-6, 0. x+3 remainder 0. Answer: x+3

records.title: Remainder Theorem
records.vocabulary: Remainder Theorem Expressions and Manipulation Algebra Evaluates f(a) and compares it with the division remainder.
records.definition: Remainder Theorem evaluates x²+x+1 at 1 to get remainder 3, and x²−1 at 1 to get 0. Graph intercept checks use this. Using a=−1 for divisor x−1 is the labelled sign slip. Remainder Theorem keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Remainder theorem: remainder = f(a). x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; The divisor must be linear in the form x - a.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.
records.example: Remainder of x^2-1 divided by x-1.: f(1)=0. Remainder 0. 0. Answer: 0

records.title: Factor Theorem
records.vocabulary: Factor Theorem Expressions and Manipulation Algebra Tests candidate roots graphically and symbolically.
records.definition: Factor Theorem tests f(2)=0 on x²−4 so x−2 is a factor, and f(−1)=2 so x+1 is not a factor of x²+5x+6. Intercept hunting uses this. Treating a non-zero f(a) as a factor is the labelled error. Factor Theorem keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Factor theorem: x - a factor iff f(a)=0. x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; Use exact substitution, not a rounded guess.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.
records.example: Is x-2 a factor of x^2-4?: f(2)=0. Yes. yes Answer: yes

records.title: Identities
records.vocabulary: Identities Expressions and Manipulation Algebra Expands both sides and compares graphs or symbolic forms.
records.definition: Identities checks (x+1)² against x²+2x+1 at x=3 as 16=16, and a+b=b+a at 2 and 5 as 7=7. Mental squares use this. Solving an identity for one x and stopping is the labelled single-solution error. Identities keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Square identity: (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2. x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; Respect any denominator or root restrictions.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.
records.example: Check (x+1)^2=x^2+2x+1 at x=3.: 16 vs 9+6+1=16. Identity holds. 16=16. Answer: 16=16

records.title: One-Step Equations
records.vocabulary: One-Step Equations Equations and Inequalities Algebra Uses a balance model to perform the same action on both sides.
records.definition: One-Step Equations subtracts 7 from x+7=12 to land on 5, and divides 3x=18 to 6. Pocket-money puzzles use this. Changing only one side is the labelled broken-scale error. One-Step Equations keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Balance rule: x + a = b => x = b - a. x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; Keep both sides balanced.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.
records.example: Solve x+7=12.: x=5. Subtract 7. 5. Answer: 5

records.title: Multi-Step Equations
records.vocabulary: Multi-Step Equations Equations and Inequalities Algebra Shows legal transformations one step at a time.
records.definition: Multi-Step Equations subtracts 3 then divides by 2 on 2x+3=11 to get x=4. Taxi fares use a fixed fee plus a rate. Dividing before removing the constant is the labelled order error. Multi-Step Equations keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Linear solving: ax + b = c => x = (c-b)/a. x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; Apply every operation to both sides.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.
records.example: Solve 2x+3=11.: 2x=8. x=4. 4. Answer: 4

records.title: Equations with Fractions
records.vocabulary: Equations with Fractions Equations and Inequalities Algebra Clears denominators and solves with domain checks.
records.definition: Equations with Fractions subtracts 1 from x/2+1=4 then multiplies by 2 to get x=6. Recipes and rates use this. Multiplying only the fraction term is the labelled skipped-term error. Equations with Fractions keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Clearing denominators: multiply both sides by the LCD. x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; Do not multiply only selected terms.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.
records.example: Solve x/2+1=4.: x/2=3. x=6. 6. Answer: 6

records.title: Literal Equations
records.vocabulary: Literal Equations Equations and Inequalities Algebra Selects a target variable and isolates it symbolically.
records.definition: Literal Equations makes R the subject of I=V/R as R=V/I, and w the subject of A=ℓw as w=A/ℓ. Science formulas use this. Dropping ℓ from A=ℓw is the labelled lost-letter error. Literal Equations keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Rearranging formula: A = lw => w = A/l, l != 0. x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; Do not divide by a variable that may be zero without a restriction.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.
records.example: Solve I=V/R for R.: R=V/I. Divide. R=V/I. Answer: R=V/I

records.title: Linear Equations
records.vocabulary: Linear Equations Equations and Inequalities Algebra Solves equations and shows the intersection of two lines.
records.definition: Linear Equations solves 2x+3=11 as x=4 and 4−x=9 as x=−5. Hourly pay is linear. Calling x²+1=5 linear is the labelled power error. Linear Equations keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Linear equation: ax + b = c. x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; The coefficient of x must not be zero for one unique solution.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.
records.example: Solve 2x+3=11.: x=4. Linear. 4. Answer: 4

records.title: Simultaneous Linear Equations
records.vocabulary: Simultaneous Linear Equations Equations and Inequalities Algebra Demonstrates substitution, elimination and graph intersection.
records.definition: Simultaneous Linear Equations adds x+y=5 to x−y=1 to get 2x=6, so (3,2). Two prices from two bills use this. Solving only one equation is the labelled half-check error. Simultaneous Linear Equations keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Common solution: both equations true. x: the unknown or variable in the lesson model; Parallel distinct lines have no common solution.
Equivalent expressions: A=B\iff A-B=0. CAS checks symbolic equality by simplifying the difference or applying valid algebraic steps.

records.title: Three-Variable Systems
records.vocabulary: Three-Variable Systems Equations and Inequalities Algebra Shows planes and their common point or line in 3D.
records.definition: Three-Variable Systems uses x=1, y=2 in x+y+z=6 to get z=3, and checks 1−1+4=4. Ticket prices for three ages use this. Claiming a unique triple from one equation is the labelled under-determined error. records.title: Piecewise Functions

Adding both formulas at once is the labelled two-case error. Piecewise Functions keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.

Piecewise rule: use the matching condition. x: the function input; f(x): the function output; Conditions should not conflict for a function.

records.title: Composite Functions
records.vocabulary: Composite Functions Functions Graphs and Functions Shows intermediate outputs through two or more functions.

Composite Functions keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.

Composition: (f o g)(x)=f(g(x)). x: the function input; f(x): the function output; Check domain restrictions after composing.
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.

records.title: Inverse Functions
records.vocabulary: Inverse Functions Functions Graphs and Functions Swaps coordinates and reflects graphs in y=x.

Inverse Functions keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.

Inverse rule: f^-1(f(x))=x. x: the function input; f(x): the function output; The original must be one-to-one on the chosen domain.

records.example: Find the inverse of f(x)=2x+3.: y=2x+3. x=2y+3. y=(x-3)/2. Answer: (x-3)/2

records.title: Even and Odd Functions
records.vocabulary: Even and Odd Functions Functions Graphs and Functions Tests and visualises y-axis or origin symmetry.

Symmetry test: even: f(-x)=f(x), odd: f(-x)=-f(x). x: the function input; f(x): the function output; A function can be neither even nor odd.
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: Is f(x)=x^2 even or odd?: f(-x)=x^2=f(x). Even. even Answer: even

records.title: Increasing and Decreasing
records.vocabulary: Increasing and Decreasing Functions Graphs and Functions Uses graph motion and derivative signs.
records.definition: Increasing and Decreasing reads 2x+1 upward from left to right and −x+4 downward. Cooling tea is decreasing in time. Reading the graph right-to-left is the labelled direction error. Increasing and Decreasing keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
