Monotonic direction: x increases => compare y. x: the function input; f(x): the function output; Flat intervals are constant, not increasing or decreasing.
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: Is y=2x+1 increasing?: Slope 2>0. y rises as x increases. Yes. Answer: yes

records.title: Periodic Functions
records.vocabulary: Periodic Functions Functions Graphs and Functions Measures period and aligns repeated cycles.
records.definition: Periodic Functions overlays one sine cycle of length 2π and checks sin(x+2π)=sin x. Tides and clocks use this. Calling any wiggle periodic is the labelled inexact-repeat error. Periodic Functions keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Period rule: f(x+T)=f(x). x: the function input; f(x): the function output; State the input unit for the period.
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: What is the period of sin x in radians?: sin(x+2π)=sin x. Period 2π. 2π. Answer: 2π

records.title: Recursive Functions
records.vocabulary: Recursive Functions Functions Graphs and Functions Builds tables and plots recursively defined terms.
records.definition: Recursive Functions builds 3, 5, 7, 9 from +2 each time. Monthly savings uses this. Starting the rule at n=1 with no a1 is the labelled missing-seed error. Recursive Functions keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Recursive rule: a_n depends on a_(n-1). x: the function input; f(x): the function output; Do not skip terms unless a direct formula is known.
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.

records.title: Vertical Translation
records.vocabulary: Vertical Translation Function Transformations Graphs and Functions Moves graphs up or down using a slider.
records.definition: Vertical Translation lifts every point of x^2 by 3, so (1,1) becomes (1,4). A base fare added to a rate uses this. Sliding the graph sideways for +3 is the labelled axis mix-up. Vertical Translation keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Vertical shift: g(x)=f(x)+k. x: the function input; f(x): the function output; The domain usually stays the same after a vertical shift.
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: Move y=x^2 up 3. Where is the vertex?: (0,0) plus 3 in y. (0,3). (0,3). Answer: (0,3)

records.title: Horizontal Translation
records.vocabulary: Horizontal Translation Function Transformations Graphs and Functions Moves graphs left or right and highlights sign convention.
records.definition: Horizontal Translation parks the old vertex of x^2 at x=2 for (x−2)^2. A delayed wave uses this. Moving f(x−2) left is the labelled sign error. Horizontal Translation keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Horizontal shift: g(x)=f(x-h). x: the function input; f(x): the function output; Track signs carefully inside the function.
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: What does f(x-2) do to y=x^2?: x-2=0 at x=2. Right 2. right 2 Answer: right 2

records.title: Vertical Stretch and Compression
records.vocabulary: Vertical Stretch and Compression Function Transformations Graphs and Functions Changes output scale and displays corresponding coordinates.
records.definition: Vertical Stretch and Compression triples the height of x^2 at x=1 from 1 to 3. Louder amplitude uses this. Changing x while stretching vertically is the labelled wrong-axis scale error. Vertical Stretch and Compression keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Vertical scale: g(x)=a f(x). x: the function input; f(x): the function output; A negative factor also reflects in the x-axis.
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: What is 3x^2 at x=1?: 3*1=3. (1,3). 3. Answer: 3

records.title: Horizontal Stretch and Compression
records.vocabulary: Horizontal Stretch and Compression Function Transformations Graphs and Functions Changes input scale and compares points.
records.definition: Horizontal Stretch and Compression copies the value 4 from x=2 on x^2 onto x=1 for (2x)^2. Faster playback uses this. Saying f(2x) stretches by 2 is the labelled direct-factor error. Horizontal Stretch and Compression keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Horizontal scale: g(x)=f(cx). x: the function input; f(x): the function output; Use positive c for basic stretch and compression here.
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: What does f(2x) do to width?: Reciprocal of 2 is 1/2. Horizontal compression. compression 1/2 Answer: compression 1/2

records.title: Reflection in x-Axis
records.vocabulary: Reflection in x-Axis Function Transformations Graphs and Functions Reflects all y-values.
records.definition: Reflection in x-Axis flips (2,3) to (2,−3) and turns a peak into a valley. Profit to loss uses this. Changing x during an x-axis flip is the labelled wrong-coordinate error. Reflection in x-Axis keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
x-axis reflection: (x,y)->(x,-y). x: the function input; f(x): the function output; Points on the x-axis do not move.
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: Reflect (2,3) in the x-axis.: Keep x=2. y becomes -3. (2,-3). Answer: (2,-3)

records.title: Reflection in y-Axis
records.vocabulary: Reflection in y-Axis Function Transformations Graphs and Functions Reflects all x-values.
records.definition: Reflection in y-Axis mirrors (2,3) to (−2,3). A left-right design uses this. Changing y during a y-axis flip is the labelled wrong-coordinate error. Reflection in y-Axis keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
y-axis reflection: (x,y)->(-x,y). x: the function input; f(x): the function output; Points on the y-axis do not move.
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: Reflect (2,3) in the y-axis.: x becomes -2. y stays 3. (-2,3). Answer: (-2,3)

records.title: Combined Transformations
records.vocabulary: Combined Transformations Function Transformations Graphs and Functions Builds transformations sequentially.
records.definition: Combined Transformations tracks (0,0) on x^2 to (1,3) on 2(x−1)^2+3. Fitted waves use this. Treating x−1 as a vertical shift is the labelled inside-outside mix-up. Combined Transformations keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Combined transform: g(x)=a f(x-h)+k. x: the function input; f(x): the function output; Order can matter when transformations are mixed.
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.

records.title: Transformation Order
records.vocabulary: Transformation Order Function Transformations Graphs and Functions Compares different orders side by side.
records.definition: Transformation Order walks 2 → 4 → 7 for ×2 then +3, and contrasts +3 then ×2 = 10. Graphics pipelines use this. Applying steps in a random order is the labelled commute error. Transformation Order keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Ordered transform: new value uses previous value. x: the function input; f(x): the function output; Follow the chosen convention consistently.
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: Double 2 then add 3.: 2*2=4. 4+3=7. 7. Answer: 7

records.title: Parameter Explorer
records.vocabulary: Parameter Explorer Function Transformations Graphs and Functions Controls all transformation parameters with sliders.
records.definition: Parameter Explorer slides a from 1 to 3 to steepen y=ax+1, then slides b to lift the intercept. Interest-rate models use parameters. Treating a as if it were the input x is the labelled role error. Parameter Explorer keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Parameter model: y=a x+b. x: the function input; f(x): the function output; Change one parameter at a time for clear evidence.
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: In y=ax+b, which parameter shifts the line vertically?: b is added to every y. b. b Answer: b

records.title: Parent-Function Library
records.vocabulary: Parent-Function Library Function Transformations Graphs and Functions Selects a parent function and applies transformations.
records.definition: Parent-Function Library names x^2 as the quadratic parent and |x| as the V parent before any shift. Graph matching starts here. Calling (x−2)^2 the parent is the labelled extra-transform error. Parent-Function Library keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Parent function: simplest family rule. x: the function input; f(x): the function output; Parent functions are chosen before shifts and stretches.
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: What is the quadratic parent?: Simplest squared rule. y=x^2. y=x^2. Answer: y=x^2

records.title: Graph Matching
records.vocabulary: Graph Matching Function Transformations Graphs and Functions Challenges learners to match slider values or expressions.
records.definition: Graph Matching checks intercept 1 and a second point (2,5) before accepting the line. Science graphs use this. Matching on a single shared point is the labelled one-point error. Graph Matching keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Match check: formula, table, and graph agree. x: the function input; f(x): the function output; Check scale and axes before deciding.
Function notation: y=f(x). Each input x is mapped to an output y shown on the graph and in the table.
records.example: For y=2x+1, what is the y-intercept?: x=0 gives 1. 1. 1. Answer: 1

records.title: Cartesian Plane
records.vocabulary: Cartesian Plane Coordinate Geometry Geometry Labels quadrants and tracks pointer coordinates.
records.definition: Cartesian Plane places (3,−2) in IV and (−3,2) in II. Maps and graphs share this grid. Swapping the coordinates to (−2,3) is the labelled order error. Cartesian Plane keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Point coordinates: (x,y). x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate; Order matters in an ordered pair.
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Which quadrant is (3,-2)?: x>0, y<0. Quadrant IV. IV. Answer: IV

records.title: Plotting Points
records.vocabulary: Plotting Points Coordinate Geometry Geometry Places points from ordered pairs and checks accuracy.
records.definition: Plotting Points walks four ticks right and one tick up to (4,1). Seat maps use the same address. Counting y first is the labelled swapped-axis error. Plotting Points keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Plotting rule: (x,y) means horizontal then vertical. x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate; Do not swap x and y.
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Plot (4,1). How far right?: x=4. 4 units right. 4. Answer: 4

records.title: Distance Between Points
records.vocabulary: Distance Between Points Coordinate Geometry Geometry Builds a right triangle and applies Pythagoras.
records.definition: Distance Between Points builds the 3-4-5 triangle from the origin to (3,4). Map legs use this. Adding 3+4=7 as the distance is the labelled skip-root error. Distance Between Points keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Distance formula: d=sqrt((x2-x1)^2+(y2-y1)^2). x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate; Use the same units on both axes.
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Distance from (0,0) to (3,4).: √(9+16)=√25. 5. 5. Answer: 5

records.title: Midpoint
records.vocabulary: Midpoint Coordinate Geometry Geometry Moves endpoints and updates midpoint coordinates.
records.definition: Midpoint averages 0 with 4 and 0 with 2 to sit at (2,1). A segment centre uses this. Using only one coordinate average is the labelled half-formula error. Midpoint keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Midpoint formula: M=((x1+x2)/2,(y1+y2)/2). x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate; Keep x and y averages separate.
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Midpoint of (0,0) and (4,2).: x-average 2. y-average 1. (2,1). Answer: (2,1)

records.title: Section Formula
records.vocabulary: Section Formula Coordinate Geometry Geometry Moves a division point and shows internal or external ratios.
records.definition: Section Formula places the 1:2 point two-thirds of the way from B, so on [0,6] it sits at 2. Map posts use this. Swapping m and n to 4 instead of 2 is the labelled ratio-order error. Section Formula keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Section formula: P=((nx1+mx2)/(m+n),(ny1+my2)/(m+n)). x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate; Use internal formula only for points between endpoints.
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: 1:1 section of (0,0) to (6,0).: Halfway. (3,0). (3,0). Answer: (3,0)

records.title: Gradient / Slope
records.vocabulary: Gradient / Slope Coordinate Geometry Geometry Displays a movable slope triangle.
records.definition: Gradient / Slope reads 4 up and 2 across as m=2 on the line through (0,1). Roads use this ratio. Subtracting in the wrong order to get −2 is the labelled flipped-rise error. Gradient / Slope keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Slope formula: m=(y2-y1)/(x2-x1). x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate; Vertical lines have undefined slope.
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Slope from (0,1) to (2,5).: Rise 4, run 2. 4/2=2. 2. Answer: 2

records.title: Equation of a Line
records.vocabulary: Equation of a Line Coordinate Geometry Geometry Switches point-slope, slope-intercept and general forms.
records.definition: Equation of a Line writes y−1=2x from (0,1) and slope 2, then checks (3,7). Two-point form uses the same slope first. Forgetting to use a point and writing only y=2x is the labelled missing-intercept error. Equation of a Line keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Slope-intercept form: y=mx+b. x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate; Vertical lines need x=c, not y=mx+b.
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Line through (0,1) with slope 2.: y-1=2x. y=2x+1. y=2x+1. Answer: y=2x+1

records.title: Parallel Lines
records.vocabulary: Parallel Lines Coordinate Geometry Geometry Constructs lines with equal slopes.
records.definition: Parallel Lines stacks y=2x+3 above y=2x with the same tilt. Rails use this. Calling any non-intersecting-looking pair parallel without checking slopes is the labelled unchecked-tilt error. Parallel Lines keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Parallel slopes: m1=m2. x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate; Vertical lines are parallel to other vertical lines.
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Are y=2x and y=2x+3 parallel?: Both slopes are 2. Yes. yes Answer: yes

records.title: Perpendicular Lines
records.vocabulary: Perpendicular Lines Coordinate Geometry Geometry Shows negative reciprocal relationships.
records.definition: Perpendicular Lines draws y=2x and y=−(1/2)x meeting at a right angle. Street grids use this. Using the same slope 2 for the perpendicular is the labelled parallel-mix error. Perpendicular Lines keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Perpendicular slopes: m1*m2=-1. x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate; The rule m1*m2=-1 applies to non-vertical slopes.
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Perpendicular slope to m=2.: -1/2. Negative reciprocal. -1/2. Answer: -1/2

records.title: Angle Between Lines
records.vocabulary: Angle Between Lines Coordinate Geometry Geometry Measures the smaller and directed angles.
records.definition: Angle Between Lines computes |(0−1)/(1+0)|=1, hence 45° between y=x and the x-axis. Road junctions use this. Subtracting slopes without the denominator is the labelled raw-difference error. Angle Between Lines keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Angle rule: parallel 0 degrees, perpendicular 90 degrees. x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate; Use the smaller angle by default.
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Angle between y=x and the x-axis.: m1=1, m2=0. tanθ=1, θ=45°. 45°. Answer: 45°

records.title: Point-to-Line Distance
records.vocabulary: Point-to-Line Distance Coordinate Geometry Geometry Drops a perpendicular and calculates its length.
records.definition: Point-to-Line Distance: Point–Line Distance plugs the origin into |−12|/5=2.4 for 3x+4y=12. Clearance around a road uses this. Forgetting the denominator 5 is the labelled un-normalised error. Point–Line Distance keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Shortest distance: perpendicular to the line. x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate; Use the line, not just a chosen endpoint.
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.

records.title: Coordinate Loci
records.vocabulary: Coordinate Loci Coordinate Geometry Geometry Moves points satisfying coordinate conditions.
records.definition: Coordinate Loci traces the circle through (5,0) and (3,4). A radar range uses this. Plotting only one point and calling it the locus is the labelled single-point error. Coordinate Loci keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Circle locus: x^2+y^2=r^2. x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate; Draw all points, not one sample point.
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Does (3,4) lie on x^2+y^2=25?: 9+16=25. Yes. yes Answer: yes

records.title: Coordinate Transformations
records.vocabulary: Coordinate Transformations Coordinate Geometry Geometry Updates coordinate rules during transformations.
records.definition: Coordinate Transformations slides (1,3) by +2 and −1 to (3,2). Map projections use this. Applying the shift to the axes labels but not the point is the labelled half-transform error. Coordinate Transformations keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Translation rule: (x,y)->(x+a,y+b). x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate; Use the same rule for the whole object.
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Map (1,3) by (x,y)→(x+2,y-1).: x becomes 3. y becomes 2. (3,2). Answer: (3,2)

records.title: Polar Coordinates
records.vocabulary: Polar Coordinates Coordinate Geometry Geometry Converts and plots points in both systems.
records.definition: Polar Coordinates converts (3,0°) to Cartesian (3,0) and (3,90°) to (0,3). Navigation bearings use this. Treating (3,90°) as (3,90) on the Cartesian grid is the labelled unconverted-pair error. Polar Coordinates keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Polar conversion: x=r cos theta, y=r sin theta. x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate; State angle units.
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Convert (r,θ)=(3,0°) to Cartesian.: x=3 cos 0=3. y=0. (3,0). Answer: (3,0)

records.title: Parametric Coordinates
records.vocabulary: Parametric Coordinates Coordinate Geometry Geometry Animates points along parameter-defined paths.
records.definition: Parametric Coordinates plots (0,0), (2,4), (3,6) as t grows. A moving particle uses this. Eliminating t incorrectly and losing the path direction is the labelled static-curve error. Parametric Coordinates keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Parametric rule: (x,y)=(x(t),y(t)). x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate; Use the given parameter range if one is stated.
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: For x=t, y=2t, find the point at t=3.: x=3, y=6. (3,6). (3,6). Answer: (3,6)

records.title: Barycentric Coordinates
records.vocabulary: Barycentric Coordinates Coordinate Geometry Geometry Adjusts weighted coordinates inside and outside a triangle.
records.definition: Barycentric Coordinates hangs equal masses 1/2,1/2,0 at A and B to sit at the midpoint. Mesh shading uses this. Using three coordinates that sum to 2 is the labelled un-normalised-mass error. Barycentric Coordinates keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Barycentric average: P=w1A+w2B+w3C, w1+w2+w3=1. x: horizontal coordinate; y: vertical coordinate; Weights for standard affine coordinates should be normalised.
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Barycentric midpoint of AB.: Weights 1/2, 1/2, 0. (1/2,1/2,0). (1/2,1/2,0). Answer: (1/2, 1/2, 0)

records.title: Vector Introduction
records.vocabulary: Vector Introduction Vectors Geometry Displays vectors as movable arrows.
records.definition: Vector Introduction draws the arrow from (0,0) to (3,4) and labels length 5. Displacement uses this. Calling <3,4> the same as the scalar 5 is the labelled lost-direction error. Vector Introduction keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Vector Introduction: v=(x,y). v: a vector
Vector magnitude: \|v\|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Magnitude is the length of the arrow from its components.
records.example: Magnitude of <3,4>.: √(9+16)=5. |v|=5. 5. Answer: 5

records.title: Component Form
records.vocabulary: Component Form Vectors Geometry Shows horizontal and vertical components.
records.definition: Component Form splits <3,4> into a 3-step east basis arrow and a 4-step north basis arrow. Force tables use this. Adding 3+4=7 as a single component is the labelled mixed-axis error. Component Form keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Component Form: v=(vx,vy). v: a vector
Vector magnitude: \|v\|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Magnitude is the length of the arrow from its components.
records.example: Write <3,4> in i,j form.: 3i+4j. Basis form. 3i+4j. Answer: 3i+4j

records.title: Position Vectors
records.vocabulary: Position Vectors Vectors Geometry Updates vector coordinates when points move.
records.definition: Position Vectors pins <2,3> to the origin so the tip is the point (2,3). GPS offsets use this. Drawing the same arrow from (1,1) and still calling it OA is the labelled misplaced-tail error. Position Vectors keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Position Vectors: OP=(x,y). v: a vector
Vector magnitude: \|v\|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Magnitude is the length of the arrow from its components.
records.example: Position vector of A(2,3).: OA=<2,3>. Tail at the origin. <2, 3>. Answer: <2, 3>

records.title: Vector Addition
records.vocabulary: Vector Addition Vectors Geometry Uses head-to-tail and parallelogram constructions.
records.definition: Vector Addition walks <1,2> then <3,4> to the tip <4,6>. Combined displacements use this. Adding magnitudes √5+5 as the resultant length is the labelled scalar-sum error. Vector Addition keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Vector Addition: u+v=(ux+vx,uy+vy). v: a vector
Vector magnitude: \|v\|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Magnitude is the length of the arrow from its components.

records.title: Vector Subtraction
records.vocabulary: Vector Subtraction Vectors Geometry Builds the vector from one endpoint to another.
records.definition: Vector Subtraction subtracts 2 from 5 and 3 from 1 to get <3,−2>. Relative position uses this. Reversing the order to <−3,2> without a reason is the labelled swapped-difference error. Vector Subtraction keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Vector Subtraction: u-v=(ux-vx,uy-vy). v: a vector
Vector magnitude: \|v\|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Magnitude is the length of the arrow from its components.

records.title: Scalar Multiplication
records.vocabulary: Scalar Multiplication Vectors Geometry Uses a slider to change magnitude and direction.
records.definition: Scalar Multiplication stretches <2,1> to <6,3> by the factor 3. Zooming a displacement uses this. Adding 3 to each component to get <5,4> is the labelled add-not-scale error. Scalar Multiplication keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Scalar Multiplication: kv=(kvx,kvy). v: a vector
Vector magnitude: \|v\|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Magnitude is the length of the arrow from its components.

records.title: Magnitude and Unit Vectors
records.vocabulary: Magnitude and Unit Vectors Vectors Geometry Calculates length and creates a unit vector.
records.definition: Magnitude and Unit Vectors divides <3,4> by 5 to get the direction-only arrow of length 1. Headings use this. Forgetting to divide and calling <3,4> a unit vector is the labelled un-normalised error. Magnitude and Unit Vectors keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Magnitude and Unit Vectors: |v|=sqrt(x^2+y^2). v: a vector
Vector magnitude: \|v\|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Magnitude is the length of the arrow from its components.

records.title: Dot Product
records.vocabulary: Dot Product Vectors Geometry Updates dot product and included angle.
records.definition: Dot Product multiplies matching components of <1,2> and <3,4> to 11. Work W=F·d uses this. Crossing the components into a 3D-style vector is the labelled product-mix error. Dot Product keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Dot Product: u dot v=uxvx+uyvy. v: a vector
Vector magnitude: \|v\|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Magnitude is the length of the arrow from its components.

records.title: Cross Product
records.vocabulary: Cross Product Vectors Geometry Constructs a normal vector in 3D.
records.definition: Cross Product sends i×j to k and gives area 6 for the 3-by-2 rectangle. Torque uses this. Treating a×b as a scalar 11 like a dot product is the labelled product-mix error. Cross Product keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Cross Product: u x v is perpendicular to u and v. v: a vector
Vector magnitude: \|v\|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Magnitude is the length of the arrow from its components.
records.example: What is i×j?: Right-hand rule. k. k. Answer: k

records.title: Vector Projection
records.vocabulary: Vector Projection Vectors Geometry Drops projections onto selected vectors.
records.definition: Vector Projection drops a perpendicular from <2,2> onto the x-axis to land at <2,0>. Force along a rail uses this. Leaving the result as the scalar 2 without the direction of b is the labelled missing-vector error. Vector Projection keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Vector Projection: proj_v u=((u dot v)/(v dot v))v. v: a vector
Vector magnitude: \|v\|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Magnitude is the length of the arrow from its components.
records.example: Project <2,2> onto <1,0>.: Shadow on the x-axis. <2, 0>. <2, 0>. Answer: <2, 0>

records.title: Linear Combinations
records.vocabulary: Linear Combinations Vectors Geometry Combines basis vectors with adjustable coefficients.
records.definition: Linear Combinations builds <2,3> from 2 steps of i and 3 steps of j. Mixing ingredients uses this. Adding the scalars 2+3=5 as the combination is the labelled scalar-collapse error. Linear Combinations keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Linear Combinations: au+bv. v: a vector
Vector magnitude: \|v\|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Magnitude is the length of the arrow from its components.

records.title: Vector Equation of a Line
records.vocabulary: Vector Equation of a Line Vectors Geometry Animates a point using r=a+tb.
records.definition: Vector Equation of a Line steps from (1,2) by <2,0> to (3,2) and (5,2). A parametric path uses this. Treating t as only 0 or 1 is the labelled segment-only error. Vector Equation of a Line keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Vector Equation of a Line: r=a+tv. v: a vector
Vector magnitude: \|v\|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Magnitude is the length of the arrow from its components.

records.title: Vector Equation of a Plane
records.vocabulary: Vector Equation of a Plane Vectors Geometry Builds a plane from a point and two directions.
records.definition: Vector Equation of a Plane keeps every point at height 3 when n is vertical. A tabletop uses this. Using a direction vector as if it were the normal is the labelled n-versus-d error. Vector Equation of a Plane keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Vector Equation of a Plane: r=a+su+tv. v: a vector
Vector magnitude: \|v\|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Magnitude is the length of the arrow from its components.

records.title: Relative Motion
records.vocabulary: Relative Motion Vectors Geometry Animates objects with relative velocities.
records.definition: Relative Motion subtracts 3 from 8 so A gains 5 km/h on B. Overtaking uses this. Adding 8+3=11 when both go east is the labelled same-direction-sum error. Relative Motion keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Relative Motion: v_relative=v_a-v_b. v: a vector
Vector magnitude: \|v\|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Magnitude is the length of the arrow from its components.
records.example: v_A=8 east, v_B=3 east. Find v_AB.: 8-3=5. 5 km/h east. 5 east Answer: 5 east

records.title: Force Vectors
records.vocabulary: Force Vectors Vectors Geometry Builds force polygons and calculates equilibrium.
records.definition: Force Vectors builds the 3-4-5 newton triangle. A tug in two directions uses this. Adding 3+4=7 N as the resultant is the labelled scalar-force error. Force Vectors keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Force Vectors: F_result=sum F_i. v: a vector
Vector magnitude: \|v\|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Magnitude is the length of the arrow from its components.
records.example: 3 N east and 4 N north. Resultant?: 3-4-5 triangle. 5 N. 5 N. Answer: 5 N

records.title: Free Point
records.vocabulary: Free Point Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Places movable points.
records.definition: Free Point drags (1,2) anywhere on the plane. A cursor position uses this. Forcing the point onto x^2+y^2=1 while calling it free is the labelled hidden-constraint error. Free Point keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Free Point: P=(x,y). A: a parent point or object
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: How many degrees of freedom has a free plane point?: x and y are independent. 2. 2. Answer: 2

records.title: Point on Object
records.vocabulary: Point on Object Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Keeps a point attached to a line, curve or shape.
records.definition: Point on Object slides (5,0) around the radius-5 circle and rejects (6,0). A bead on a wire uses this. Dragging off the object and keeping the old label is the labelled broken-bind error. Point on Object keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Point on Object: P on object. A: a parent point or object
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Is (5,0) on x^2+y^2=25?: 25+0=25. Yes. yes Answer: yes

records.title: Intersection Point
records.vocabulary: Intersection Point Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Creates exact intersections dynamically.
records.definition: Intersection Point sets x+1=−x+3 to get 2x=2, so (1,2). Crossing streets use this. Reading only one line and guessing (0,1) is the labelled half-system error. Intersection Point keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Intersection Point: object A meets object B. A: a parent point or object
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.

records.title: Midpoint or Centre
records.vocabulary: Midpoint or Centre Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Creates midpoints and centres of segments or conics.
records.definition: Midpoint or Centre averages −4 with 4 and 2 with −1 to sit at (0, 1/2). A diameter’s centre uses this. Using only the x-average (0,2) is the labelled forgotten-y error. Midpoint or Centre keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Midpoint or Centre: M=((x1+x2)/2,(y1+y2)/2). A: a parent point or object
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Midpoint of (-4,2) and (4,-1).: x-average 0. y-average 0.5. (0, 0.5). Answer: (0, 0.5)

records.title: Attach / Detach Point
records.vocabulary: Attach / Detach Point Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Switches between free and constrained movement.
records.definition: Attach / Detach Point: Attach / Detach locks a bead onto the circle, then unlocks it so (6,0) becomes legal. Construction tools use this. Moving an attached point off the object without detaching is the labelled broken-parent error. Attach / Detach keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Attach / Detach Point: attach means constrain. A: a parent point or object
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: An attached point on r=5: is (6,0) legal?: 36≠25. Still attached. No. Answer: no

records.title: Line Through Two Points
records.vocabulary: Line Through Two Points Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Creates a line that updates as points move.
records.definition: Line Through Two Points computes (5−1)/(2−0)=2 and writes y=2x+1. A ruler edge uses this. Drawing a second line through the same pair is the labelled uniqueness error. Line Through Two Points keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Line Through Two Points: line AB. A: a parent point or object
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.

records.title: Segment
records.vocabulary: Segment Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Creates measurable segments.
records.definition: Segment paints only the closed interval from A to B of length 5. A cut board uses this. Extending past B as if the segment were a line is the labelled infinite-extend error. Segment keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Segment: segment AB. A: a parent point or object
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Length of the segment from (0,0) to (5,0).: Δx=5. 5. 5. Answer: 5

records.title: Segment with Given Length
records.vocabulary: Segment with Given Length Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Creates a segment using numeric input.
records.definition: Segment with Given Length: Segment of Given Length opens the compass to 5 and marks the same span on a new ray. Scale drawings use this. Guessing the mark at 3 is the labelled uncopied-length error. Segment of Given Length keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Segment with Given Length: AB = fixed length. A: a parent point or object
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Copy length 5 onto a ray. How far is the new end?: The compass opening is 5. 5. 5. Answer: 5

records.title: Ray
records.vocabulary: Ray Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Creates a ray from an endpoint through another point.
records.definition: Ray shades t≥0 from the origin through 4, including 8 and excluding −2. A torch beam uses this. Including −2 on the same ray is the labelled opposite-half error. Ray keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Ray: ray AB. A: a parent point or object
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Ray from 0 through 4: is 8 on the ray?: 8=2*4, t=2≥0. Yes. yes Answer: yes

records.title: Polyline
records.vocabulary: Polyline Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Builds editable paths.
records.definition: Polyline adds 3 then 4 to walk a 7-unit path through A-B-C. A hiking trail uses this. Calling the open chain a polygon is the labelled missing-close error. Polyline keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Polyline: A-B-C. A: a parent point or object
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Path A-B-C with lengths 3 and 4. Path length?: 3+4=7. 7. 7. Answer: 7

records.title: Perpendicular Line
records.vocabulary: Perpendicular Line Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Builds a perpendicular through a selected point.
records.definition: Perpendicular Line drops y=−x/2 against y=2x at the origin. An altitude uses this. Copying slope 2 for the new line is the labelled parallel-not-perp error. Perpendicular Line keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Perpendicular Line: l perpendicular m. A: a parent point or object
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Perpendicular to y=2x through the origin.: m=-1/2. y=-x/2. y=-x/2. Answer: y=-x/2

records.title: Parallel Line
records.vocabulary: Parallel Line Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Builds a parallel through a selected point.
records.definition: Parallel Line copies slope 2 and pins the intercept at 3. A second rail uses this. Changing the slope to pass through the point is the labelled tilted-copy error. Parallel Line keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Parallel Line: l parallel m. A: a parent point or object
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Parallel to y=2x through (0,3).: Same slope 2. y=2x+3. y=2x+3. Answer: y=2x+3

records.title: Perpendicular Bisector
records.vocabulary: Perpendicular Bisector Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Constructs the bisector of a segment.
records.definition: Perpendicular Bisector stands x=2 on the midpoint of [0,4]. A circumcentre construction uses this. Drawing any perpendicular that misses the midpoint is the labelled off-centre error. Perpendicular Bisector keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Perpendicular Bisector: perpendicular at midpoint. A: a parent point or object
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Perp bisector of (0,0) and (4,0).: Midpoint (2,0). Vertical line x=2. x=2. Answer: x=2

records.title: Angle Bisector
records.vocabulary: Angle Bisector Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Constructs internal or external bisectors.
records.definition: Angle Bisector cuts 80° into 40° and 40°. A fair share of a corner uses this. Guessing 30° and 50° is the labelled unequal-split error. Angle Bisector keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Angle Bisector: angle A split equally. A: a parent point or object
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Bisect an 80° angle.: 80/2=40. Two 40° angles. 40° and 40°. Answer: 40°, 40°

records.title: Tangent
records.vocabulary: Tangent Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Creates tangents to circles, conics or functions.
records.definition: Tangent stands x=5 against the radius to (5,0). A wheel on a road uses this. Drawing a secant that cuts twice and calling it a tangent is the labelled two-hit error. Tangent keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Tangent: tangent perpendicular radius. A: a parent point or object
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Tangent at (5,0) on x^2+y^2=25.: Radius is along the x-axis. Tangent x=5. x=5. Answer: x=5

records.title: Best-Fit Line
records.vocabulary: Best-Fit Line Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Creates a regression line from selected points.
records.definition: Best-Fit Line threads a slope near 1.5 through the cloud (1,2), (2,3), (3,5). Data trends use this. Forcing the line through all three points when they are non-collinear is the labelled exact-fit error. Best-Fit Line keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Linear model: y=mx+b. m: slope; b: intercept
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Must a best-fit line pass through every data point?: It minimises residuals. No. no Answer: no

records.title: Triangle Constructor
records.vocabulary: Triangle Constructor Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Creates and manipulates triangles.
records.definition: Triangle Constructor locks 3-4-5 and checks the triangle inequality 3+4>5. Truss design uses this. Building 1-2-5 anyway is the labelled inequality error. Triangle Constructor keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Triangle angle sum: A+B+C=180 degrees. A: first angle; B: second angle; C: third angle
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Do sides 3,4,5 form a triangle?: 3+4>5 and 9+16=25. Yes, right-angled. yes Answer: yes

records.title: Regular Polygon
records.vocabulary: Regular Polygon Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Builds a polygon from a side and side count.
records.definition: Regular Polygon lists 60° exteriors around a hexagon. Tile floors use this. Using 360°/5=72° on a hexagon is the labelled wrong-n error. Regular Polygon keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Regular polygon exterior angle: exterior angle=360 degrees/n. n: number of sides; n >= 3
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Exterior angle of a regular hexagon.: 360/6=60. 60°. 60°. Answer: 60°

records.title: Rigid Polygon
records.vocabulary: Rigid Polygon Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Allows translation and rotation without deformation.
records.definition: Rigid Polygon slides a 3-4-5 tile without changing 3, 4, or 5. A robot plate uses this. Stretching a side during a drag is the labelled flexible-body error. Rigid Polygon keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Rigid invariant: lengths and angles stay equal. lengths: all side lengths; angles: all interior angles
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: After a rigid turn, what are sides 3,4,5?: Distances are preserved. 3,4,5. 3, 4, 5 Answer: 3, 4, 5

records.title: General Polygon
records.vocabulary: General Polygon Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Creates polygons from selected vertices.
records.definition: General Polygon adds 2+3+4+5=14 after closing D to A. A land boundary uses this. Leaving D-A open and still calling it a polygon is the labelled open-chain error. General Polygon keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Polygon perimeter: P=sum of side lengths. P: perimeter
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Perimeter of sides 2,3,4,5.: 2+3+4+5=14. Need the closing side included. 14. Answer: 14

records.title: Circle: Centre and Point
records.vocabulary: Circle: Centre and Point Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Updates radius as the boundary point moves.
records.definition: Circle: Centre and Point opens the compass from the origin to (3,4) and swings radius 5. A garden rope uses this. Moving P off the circle while keeping the old r label is the labelled stale-radius error. Circle: Centre and Point keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Circle radius: r=distance(C,P). r: radius; C: centre; P: point on circle
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.

records.title: Circle: Centre and Radius
records.vocabulary: Circle: Centre and Radius Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Builds a circle from numeric radius.
records.definition: Circle: Centre and Radius types r=4 and refuses (5,0). A sprinkler range uses this. Entering the diameter 8 as r is the labelled diameter-as-radius error. Circle: Centre and Radius keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Circle equation idea: distance(C,X)=r. C: centre; X: point on circle; r: fixed radius
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Circle centre (0,0), r=4. Is (4,0) on it?: Distance 4. Yes. yes Answer: yes

records.title: Circle Through Three Points
records.vocabulary: Circle Through Three Points Dynamic Geometry Constructions Geometry Builds the unique circle through three non-collinear points.
records.definition: Circle Through Three Points meets the perpendicular bisectors of (0,0)(6,0) and (0,0)(0,8) at (3,4). A triangle’s circumcircle uses this. Trying three collinear fence posts is the labelled collinear-circle error. Circle Through Three Points keeps one numerical story on the labelled chart, the interactive probe, and the three worked calculations so the original interaction canvas does not have to change.
records.formula:
Circumcircle condition: CA=CB=CC. C: circle centre; A,B,C: three points on the circle
Distance: d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}. Point movement changes lengths according to horizontal and vertical differences.
records.example: Circumcentre of (0,0),(6,0),(0,8).: Bisectors x=3 and y=4. (3,4). (3,4). Answer: (3,4)
